title: Checkpoint: Mental Shortcuts
objective: After this level you can explain why the mind uses shortcuts and how the research showed where they go wrong.
summary: Heuristics save time and effort and usually work, but their errors are systematic. That is how researchers caught them, and why some findings held up while others fell.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: why would a smart mind cut corners?
cards.body: You've watched shortcuts misfire, from a rigged wheel to a slow walk down a hallway. Now the bigger picture: why the mind uses them at all, and how researchers caught them in the act.

cards.headline: Useful, but predictably wrong
cards.body: Tversky and Kahneman put it plainly in 1974: in general, heuristics are quite useful, but sometimes they lead to severe and systematic errors. A rule of thumb saves time and energy, even though it isn't always the best method. Klayman and Ha said the same about testing ideas: the positive test strategy is often a very good heuristic under realistic conditions.

cards.headline: Caught by their mistakes
cards.body: How do you study a shortcut you can't see? By its errors. Kahneman explained that heuristics were identified by the characteristic errors they cause, and because those errors are systematic, they are predictable. Set up a question where the shortcut and the right answer part ways, then watch which one people give. The wheel, Linda and the 2-4-6 puzzle all work that way.

items.label: Held up
points: Word priming: related words are recognized faster

items.label: Fell or shrank
points: Slow-walking priming: no effect with infrared timing (2012)
Dunning-Kruger: may be much smaller than reported (2020)

items.label: Still argued
points: Linda: frequency formats alone did not remove the effect (2001)

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: Why the mind relies on fast shortcuts, and how researchers catch them by the errors they cause.
How availability, anchoring, representativeness and the halo effect bend everyday judgments.
What Wason's puzzle, hindsight studies and driver ratings show about checking our own beliefs.
Which findings held up, like anchoring, and which shrank or failed, like slow-walking priming.

questions.prompt: Mental Shortcuts recap: how did Tversky and Kahneman sum up heuristics in 1974?

options.label: Harmless, because their errors are random
options.rationale: The errors are systematic, not random.

options.label: Quite useful, but sometimes badly wrong
Always misleading and best avoided
options.rationale: They called heuristics quite useful in general.

options.label: Useful only for trained experts

questions.explanation: In general heuristics are quite useful, but sometimes they lead to severe and systematic errors.

questions.prompt: Mental Shortcuts recap: why can researchers study a shortcut they can't observe directly?

options.label: Brain scans show each heuristic at work
options.rationale: The method in this chapter is setting traps for predictable errors.

options.label: People can accurately report their own shortcuts
options.rationale: Level 55's students misreported even their own ratings.

options.label: Shortcuts only appear in laboratory puzzles
options.rationale: They show up in judging risks and rating drivers too.

options.label: Their errors are systematic, so they can be predicted

questions.explanation: Heuristics are identified by the characteristic errors they cause, and systematic errors can be predicted and tested.

questions.prompt: Mental Shortcuts recap, from Level 53: what did the rigged wheel of fortune show?

options.label: Students ignored the meaningless number
Paying for accuracy removed the effect
An arbitrary number pulled estimates toward it
Only students who saw 65 were affected
options.rationale: Both groups were pulled toward their own number.

questions.explanation: Students who saw 10 guessed a median of 25 percent; those who saw 65 guessed 45.

questions.prompt: Mental Shortcuts recap, from Level 56: what did most people do in Wason's 2-4-6 puzzle?

options.label: Tested sets they expected to fail
options.rationale: That would have helped, but few did it.

options.label: Tested sets that fit their own guess
Found the rule on the first try
options.rationale: Only 6 of 29 got it without a wrong announcement.

options.label: Refused to announce any rule
options.rationale: Most announced a rule, often a wrong one.

questions.explanation: They tested sets like 6, 8, 10 that fit their guess, which could never show it was too narrow.

questions.prompt: Mental Shortcuts recap, from Level 59: which priming finding holds up well?

options.label: Old-age words make people walk slower
Flag images shift political views
options.rationale: Flag priming failed in Many Labs.

options.label: Images of money shift beliefs about society
options.rationale: Currency priming failed in Many Labs.

options.label: Related words are recognized faster

questions.explanation: Word priming is robust: a word like cat makes a related word like dog quicker to recognize.
